blocks.text: “There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music.

As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”

While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other.

From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks.

In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition.

Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared.

Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II.

A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”

The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap.

On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life.

A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine.

At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. After having your portrait taken, what better than to take a shot at a portrait? That is what Mat Jacob’s shooting stand offers, soberly titled “Innocentes photos de merde” (Innocent Crappy Photos). A tribute to the images that regularly appear before the court of public opinion and suffer, too, the violence of technology. Fire!

And to restore some calm to all this, nothing beats soothing your heart by leaving with the photograph of one of your own pulses. The experience is made possible by the laboratory of the Trigone team, a member of the Lux network, which parks its caravan at Zone i for the bicentenary of photography. By bringing the electrical pulse of a heartbeat into dialogue with the movement of photons on a sensitive surface, the photographic process here transfigures one’s own heart into an image. These devices all remind us that Zone i remains above all a sensory experience, more than just a festival, and reflect the place’s determination, voiced by Mat Jacob: “to bring photography to life, whether it’s serious or not.”
